title: Webhooks & Observability: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on reliable webhook delivery, signature verification, idempotent consumers, and production observability with structured logs, correlation IDs, RED metrics and OpenTelemetry tracing.

chapters.title: Webhooks and Delivery Retries
points: Webhook = provider sends an HTTP POST to your URL when an event occurs (push, not polling); the consumer must return 2xx fast
Delivery guarantee is at-least-once, never exactly-once: duplicates and out-of-order events are normal
Retry policy: any non-2xx or timeout triggers retry with exponential backoff plus jitter (e.g. 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h) up to a max, then dead-letter or disable the endpoint
Ack-then-process: verify, enqueue the payload, return 200 immediately; do heavy work in a background worker to avoid provider timeouts (often 5-10s)
Mistake: returning 500 for permanently bad payloads causes endless retries; use 2xx for 'accepted but ignored' and 4xx only for truly invalid requests

chapters.title: HMAC Signatures and Timestamps
points: HMAC-SHA256(secret, signed_payload) is sent in a header; consumer recomputes it and compares to prove authenticity and integrity
Signed payload is usually `timestamp + '.' + rawBody`; including the timestamp binds the signature to a point in time
Verify against the RAW request bytes, not re-serialized JSON: a body parser that reparses changes whitespace/key order and breaks the signature
Reject if |now - timestamp| exceeds a tolerance (about 5 minutes) to block replay attacks; replay protection needs the timestamp inside the signature
Compare with constant-time equality (crypto.timingSafeEqual / hmac.compare_digest), never ==; support secret rotation by accepting multiple signatures

chapters.title: Idempotent Consumers
points: Idempotent = processing the same event N times has the same effect as processing it once; required because delivery is at-least-once
Dedupe on the provider's unique event ID (e.g. `evt_123`), not on payload hash or arrival time
Insert the event ID into a table with a UNIQUE constraint in the same DB transaction as the side effect; a duplicate-key error means skip and return 200
Check-then-insert (SELECT then INSERT) races under concurrent retries; rely on the unique constraint or an atomic `SET NX` in Redis with a TTL
Handle out-of-order events by comparing version/timestamp or re-fetching current state from the provider API instead of trusting the payload order

chapters.title: Structured Logs and Correlation IDs
points: Structured log = one JSON object per line with fixed keys (ts, level, msg, service, event_id, request_id, duration_ms) so logs are queryable, not grep-only
Correlation ID: generate at the edge (or accept inbound `X-Request-ID`), store in request-scoped context (AsyncLocalStorage / contextvars), attach to every log line
Propagate the ID on all outbound calls and queue messages, and return it in the response header so support can trace one request across services
Log event_id, status code, and latency for each webhook delivery so a failed delivery can be located by ID in seconds
Mistake: logging secrets, signatures, tokens or full PII payloads; redact them, and use levels consistently (info for normal, error only for actionable failures)

chapters.title: RED Metrics and OpenTelemetry Tracing
points: RED = Rate (requests/sec), Errors (failed requests/sec or ratio), Duration (latency distribution); use for every request-driven service (USE is for resources)
Report duration as a histogram and alert on percentiles (p95/p99), never the average, which hides tail latency
Keep metric label cardinality low: label by route template (`/users/:id`), method, status class; never by user ID or raw URL (explodes time series)
OpenTelemetry trace = tree of spans sharing a trace_id; context propagates between services via the W3C `traceparent` header (version-traceid-spanid-flags)
Instrument with auto-instrumentation plus manual spans around key work, export via OTLP to a Collector, and link logs by injecting trace_id/span_id into each log line

chapters.title: Webhooks and Observability Cheat Sheet
points: Receiver flow: read raw body → verify HMAC + timestamp → dedupe event ID → enqueue → return 2xx fast
Signature: HMAC-SHA256(secret, `t.rawBody`), constant-time compare, 5-minute tolerance, rotate secrets with dual verification
Retries: exponential backoff + jitter, at-least-once delivery, dead-letter after max attempts; 2xx = done, 5xx/timeout = retry
Observability trio: JSON logs with request_id/trace_id, RED metrics (histograms, low-cardinality labels), OTel traces via `traceparent` + OTLP
Top mistakes: parsing body before verifying, check-then-insert dedupe, slow synchronous handlers, high-cardinality labels, logging secrets
